# OPENING: Christ had no biological father

**Position [L4].** Jesus Christ had a mother, Mary, and no human biological father. His conception was the work of the Holy Ghost, and Joseph stood to him as husband of his mother and legal father only. By "biological father" I mean a man whose seed generated the child. The case runs from the text's own verbs, prepositions and pronouns.

## 1. Matthew's genealogy stops "begat" at Joseph

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** In Matthew 1:2-16 every link uses ἐγέννησεν (*egennēsen*, G1080, "begat, fathered"). The last link does not. Joseph is called ἀνήρ (*anēr*, G435, "husband"), and the birth is "of whom" (ἐξ ἧς, *ex hēs*), with ἐκ (*ek*, G1537) meaning "out of, from the source" and the relative pronoun feminine singular. Jesus came out of Mary, not out of Joseph.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:12 shows the writer uses "begat" freely: "Jechonias begat Salathiel". Where he means a father's generation he says so. At Joseph he changes the construction.

**[L4]** Two footings carry this: the repeated verb in Matthew 1:12 and the verb and feminine pronoun in Matthew 1:16 [L2]. The writer who writes "begat" thirty-nine times declines it at the last link, and he assigns the birth to the woman by gender. So the genealogy is a legal line through Joseph and not a claim of generation by him.

## 2. The conception preceded the coming together, and its source was the Holy Ghost

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** συνελθεῖν (*synelthein*, G4905) means "to come together" as husband and wife. The text places the pregnancy before that. The source is ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (*ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of the Holy Spirit").

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** γεννηθέν (*gennēthen*, G1080, "begotten, conceived") is the same root as "begat" in the genealogy. The angel assigns the begetting of the child to the Holy Ghost, with the same preposition ἐκ ("out of").

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

**[L2]** ἐγίνωσκεν (*eginōsken*, G1097, "knew") is the verb for sexual knowledge. Joseph did not know her through to the birth.

**[L4]** The three verses give a chain. Pregnancy came before any coming together (Matthew 1:18, *synelthein*). The begetting is from the Holy Ghost (Matthew 1:20, *ek*). Joseph did not know her until the birth (Matthew 1:25, *eginōsken*). So no male act of Joseph's, nor any other man's, entered the conception.

## 3. Mary says "I know not a man," and the angel names the agent

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω (*andra ou ginōskō*, "a man I do not know") is her stated reason for asking. The angel answers with two verbs: ἐπελεύσεται (*epeleusetai*, G1904, "shall come upon") and ἐπισκιάσει (*episkiasei*, G1982, "shall overshadow"). Both name the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest as agent. No man is named.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son." The Greek is παρθένος (*parthenos*, G3933, "virgin"). It quotes Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son." The Hebrew there is הָעַלְמָה (*ha-almah*, H5959, "the young woman of marriageable age, unmarried"). The same word stands in Genesis 24:43, "when the virgin cometh forth to draw water," of Rebekah, who is described in Genesis 24:16 as "a virgin, neither had any man known her."

**[L4]** Mary's question rests on "I know not a man" [L1, Luke 1:34]. The angel supplies an agent that is not a man [L1, Luke 1:35]. Matthew applies *parthenos* to the conception [L3, Matthew 1:23]. So the angel's answer excludes a man's contribution by what it supplies in place of one.

## 4. Fatherhood of God is not physical generation, and the text separates Joseph's role

**[L1]** John 4:24: "God is a Spirit."

**[L3]** Luke 24:39: "a spirit hath not flesh and bones."

**[L4]** Both verses fix the nature of God as Spirit without flesh and bones [L1, L3]. So the begetting by the Holy Ghost in Matthew 1:20 cannot be a biological act. The word "father" for God means a divine origin, not a physical one. The child's flesh is attributed to the mother.

**[L1]** Hebrews 10:5: "a body hast thou prepared me."

**[L2]** κατηρτίσω (*katērtisō*, from καταρτίζω, G2675, "to fit, prepare") says the body was prepared for him.

**[L1]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman."

**[L2]** γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (*genomenon ek gynaikos*, "made out of a woman") names only the woman as source, with the same *ek* as in Matthew 1:16.

**Joseph's place.** **[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph." **[L2]** ἐνομίζετο (*enomizeto*, G3543, "was reckoned, supposed by custom") marks the relation as a supposition and not a fact of generation. **[L1]** Luke 2:48: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." **[L3]** Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my father's business?" The child corrects the term "father" and applies it to God. Luke 2:33 shows the narrator's own usage: "Joseph and his mother marvelled." The narrator does not call Joseph his father. **[L4]** The footings are the *enomizeto* of Luke 3:23 [L2] and the child's own correction in Luke 2:49 [L3]. Joseph's "fatherhood" is legal and reputed. It is not biological.

## 5. The Davidic line is secured without Joseph's seed

**[L1]** Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."

**[L2]** σπέρματος (*spermatos*, G4690, "seed") and κατὰ σάρκα (*kata sarka*, "according to the flesh") fix a bodily descent from David. The Holy Ghost is not a David descendant, so the descent must come through the mother.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:12 puts Joseph in the line of Jechonias. Jeremiah 22:30 says of him: "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David." The Hebrew זֶרַע (*zera*, H2233, "seed") is the same word as in Genesis 3:15: "thy seed and her seed."

**[L4]** The footings are *spermatos kata sarka* in Romans 1:3 [L2] and the *zera* sentence in Jeremiah 22:30 [L3]. Jesus is of David's seed in the flesh without being the seed of Jechonias through Joseph. That resolves the apparent conflict only if the flesh came from Mary. Luke 1:32 gives "the throne of his father David" by legal succession through Joseph, as Matthew 1:20 addresses him: "Joseph, thou son of David".

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on

1. Matthew's genealogy breaks the "begat" pattern at Joseph. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:16 "of whom was born Jesus" with [L2] ἐγέννησεν (*egennēsen*, "begat") against ἐξ ἧς (*ex hēs*, "out of whom," feminine), and [L3] Matthew 1:12 "Jechonias begat Salathiel" showing that the writer uses "begat" where he means fathering.
2. The conception preceded any coming together of Joseph and Mary and was from the Holy Ghost. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18 "before they came together" with [L2] συνελθεῖν (*synelthein*, "to come together") and ἐκ (*ek*, "out of"), [L1] Matthew 1:20, and [L3] Matthew 1:25 "knew her not till she had brought forth".
3. Mary's "I know not a man" is answered by the Holy Ghost as agent, not a man. Footing: [L1] Luke 1:34-35 with [L2] ἐπισκιάσει (*episkiasei*, "shall overshadow") and παρθένος (*parthenos*, "virgin"), and [L3] Matthew 1:23 and Isaiah 7:14.
4. God's fatherhood of the child is not physical generation, and Joseph's fatherhood is only reputed or legal. Footing: [L1] John 4:24 "God is a Spirit" with [L3] Luke 24:39 "a spirit hath not flesh and bones," [L2] ἐνομίζετο (*enomizeto*, "was supposed") in [L1] Luke 3:23, and [L3] Luke 2:49.
5. The child's flesh came from Mary and his Davidic descent is bodily through her. Footing: [L1] Galatians 4:4 "made of a woman" with [L2] ἐκ γυναικός (*ek gynaikos*, "out of a woman"), [L1] Romans 1:3 with [L2] σπέρματος (*spermatos*, "seed"), and [L3] Jeremiah 22:30.
6. Answer to the question: Christ had no biological father. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 and [L1] Luke 1:34-35 with [L2] ἐκ (*ek*, "out of") and ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω (*andra ou ginōskō*, "a man I know not"), carried by links 1 to 5 [L4].

## PRESS ON D1: Matthew 1:16, the passive and the husband

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** The verse that turns to the passive *egennēthē* (G1080, "was born") with *ex hēs* (feminine, "of whom") also names Joseph as *anēr* (G435, "husband"). The mother is named as the one who bore. The husband stands in the same verse.

**[L3]** "Born of" a woman is said of a man whose father is named. Matthew 11:11: "Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist." John's father is named at Luke 1:13: "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John."

**[L3]** The writer's very next address to Joseph names his line. Matthew 1:20: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]"

**[L4]** The footings are the passive with its named husband [L2, Matthew 1:16] and the "born of women" usage of a fathered man [L3, Matthew 11:11 with Luke 1:13]. A passive with the mother as source speaks of a fathered child elsewhere in the same Gospel. So the change of verb at 1:16 states the birth from the mother, and the line Matthew writes, a "begat" line (Matthew 1:12, "Jechonias begat Salathiel"), ends at "Joseph the husband of Mary." The verse fits a named father. The defender's "legal line" is a category Matthew 1:2-16 does not use.

## PRESS ON D2: the timing rows read in Matthew's own order

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband..." **[L1]** Matthew 1:24: "Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife."

**[L2]** *synelthein* (G4905, "to come together") is set by what Matthew narrates next: "took unto him his wife" (1:24), her coming into his house.

**[L3]** The law names that same step as a distinct act after betrothal. Deuteronomy 20:7: "what man [is there] that hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her?" The law also calls the betrothed damsel a wife. Deuteronomy 22:24: "he hath humbled his neighbour's wife."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."

**[L2]** *ouk eginōsken autēn heōs hou eteken* ("knew her not till she brought forth") carries the abstinence up to the birth. In Matthew's order it follows the taking of 1:24.

**[L4]** The footings are Matthew's sequence [L1, 1:18, 1:24, 1:25] and the law's two steps, betrothed and then taken [L3, Deuteronomy 20:7], with *synelthein* [L2]. Three things follow:
- Matthew 1:18 dates the finding before the taking into his house.
- Matthew 1:25 covers the time after the taking.
- Joseph is "her husband" (1:19) and she is "Mary thy wife" (1:20) from the espousal.

The defender's link joins 1:25 to the time before 1:24, and Matthew's order does not join them.

**On "of the Holy Ghost" (*ek*):**
- **[L2]** Matthew 1:20's margin gives *gennaō*, "begotten."
- **[L3]** The same *ek* with the same verb is said of believers. 1 John 5:1: "every one that loveth him that begat loveth him also that is begotten of him." John 1:13 says of believers: "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God."
- **[L4]** Both of those verses use *ek* with God for covenant origin, said of men who have fathers. The row that carries "of the Holy Ghost" names "Joseph, thou son of David" and "Mary thy wife" in the same sentence. It fits the named father.

## PRESS ON D3: Luke 1:34-35 at the word level

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *andra ou ginōskō* is present active indicative, "I do not know." It states her condition when the angel spoke, a virgin "espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David" (Luke 1:27, *parthenos*). The word names her state at the annunciation.

**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2] and [L3]** The two verbs, at their other rows:
- *eperchomai* (G1904, "come upon"). Acts 1:8: "ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me." These are the apostles, empowered.
- *episkiazō* (G1982, "overshadow"). Luke 9:34: "there came a cloud, and overshadowed them." Acts 5:15: "that at the least the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them."

**[L4]** At those rows [L3] the same verbs [L2] are empowerment and presence. The defender's "excludes a man's contribution" makes these verbs supply a begetting, and they supply that nowhere else.

**The "therefore" (*dio kai*).** The *dio kai* in verse 35 connects back to verse 32, not forward to biological divine paternity.
- **[L1]** Luke 1:32, given before Mary's question: "He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David."
- **[L3]** The title's source names a son with a man for his father. 2 Samuel 7:14: "I will be his father, and he shall be my son." 1 Chronicles 28:6 gives the son David begat and God's title in one verse: "Solomon thy son, he shall build my house and my courts: for I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father."
- **[L3]** Psalm 2:7, "Thou [art] my Son; this day have I begotten thee," is applied in the New Testament on three occasions:
  - the resurrection, Acts 13:33: "he hath raised up Jesus again; as it is also written in the second psalm, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee";
  - the priesthood, Hebrews 5:5: "Christ glorified not himself to be made an high priest; but he that said unto him, Thou art my Son, to day have I begotten thee";
  - beside 2 Samuel 7:14, Hebrews 1:5: "Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee? And again, I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son?"

**Isaiah 7:14.**
- **[L2]** The Hebrew is *ha-almah* (H5959, "the young woman"). The defender's own witness shows the difference. Genesis 24:43 uses *almah*. Genesis 24:16, where Moses states virginity, uses *bethulah* (H1330, "virgin") and adds "neither had any man known her."
- **[L3]** Isaiah's sign is bounded in Isaiah's day. Isaiah 7:16: "before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings." Isaiah 8:3: "And I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son. [went: Heb. approached]"
- **[L4]** Matthew's application stands (Matthew 1:23). The prophecy he applies [L1, Isaiah 7:14] is fulfilled in its own chapter by a conception through a man's approach [L3, Isaiah 8:3]. It fits a fathered child.

**[L1]** John 4:24, "God is a Spirit," with **[L3]** Luke 24:39, "a spirit hath not flesh and bones." I hold both as written.

**[L1] and [L2]** The flesh of the promised son is "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh" (Acts 2:30). *osphys* (G3751) is "loins, procreative power."

**[L3]** The seed is in the father's loins. Hebrews 7:10: "For he was yet in the loins of his father."

**[L4]** A spirit hath not flesh [L1, L3]. The text places flesh-seed in a father's loins [L2, Acts 2:30; L3, Hebrews 7:10]. So the defender's own verses require the child's flesh to come from a man's loins.

- **[L2]** *enomizeto* (G3543) is the same form as Acts 16:13, "where prayer was wont to be made." The word means custom, and it carries no verdict of its own.

- **[L3]** The town says: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" (John 6:42).

## ANSWER ON D1: Matthew 1:16

**[L1]** Matthew 1:3: "And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar". **[L1]** Matthew 1:5: "Booz begat Obed of Ruth".

**[L2]** G1080 *gennaō* is "to procreate (properly, of the father, but by extension of the mother)". In Matthew 1:3 and 1:5 the mother is named, yet the father stays the subject of the active *egennēsen* (begat). Naming a mother does not remove the father's verb.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus".

**[L2]** At the last link the active verb passes to Jacob and Joseph. The birth of Jesus is the passive *egennēthē* (was born) with *ex hēs*, "out of whom" (feminine singular). No man is the subject of "begat" for Jesus.
